title: L4 Capstone: The Safe Bank
story: You've reached the summit of safety. Contracts guarantee correctness. Ownership guarantees memory safety. Together, they make XIOM code that can't crash, can't leak, and can't produce wrong results. This is what professional systems programming looks like. Welcome to the end of bugs as you knew them.
why: A complete banking system demonstrates every concept from L4 — invariants, requires, ensures, ownership, borrows, and composition — in a real-world domain where correctness is non-negotiable.
analogy: The Safe Bank is your black belt test. Every technique from L4 comes together: the stance (invariants), the strikes (requires), the blocks (ensures), and the footwork (ownership). Execute the kata perfectly, and you're ready for L5.
try_it: Add a `Bank` type that holds a `Vec[Account]` with an invariant that all account IDs are unique. Add `Bank.transfer_by_id` that takes two account IDs and an amount, finds the accounts, and calls `transfer`. Every operation must have contracts. This is a real mini-banking system.
tips: The invariant `balance >= 0.0` is the single most important line — every operation must preserve it
`transfer` is the most dangerous function — both accounts are `&mut`, so the borrow checker prevents interference
`print_statement` takes `&Account` — it can run concurrently with other `&Account` borrows
Every contract in this system was designed BEFORE the body — that's Design by Contract in action
common_mistakes: Subtracting from `from` BEFORE checking `amount <= from.balance` — reorder so the check guards the mutation
Forgetting `ensures` on `transfer` — without it, you can't prove money is conserved
Opening two accounts with the same ID — a real system would need a uniqueness invariant, but that's L5's collections challenge
